insight.headline: On real data, the naive baseline wins
insight.body: Forecasting 6 months of actual published BLS data, carrying the last value forward scored 0.34% MAPE - better than sarima. The real index is close to a random walk, so added model complexity is not paying for itself at this horizon.

noiseFloor.note: The generator injects AR(1) noise, so a portion of every future price is unpredictable by construction. This floor is what a perfect model would score. Per-part error near the floor is as good as the data allows. The aggregate mean-price line is a different matter: idiosyncratic noise averages out across parts, so any visible gap there is systematic model error, not noise.

futureTest.disclaimer: Hidden months come from the same generative process as the training months. This measures how well each model recovers a known process at each horizon - a valid comparison between models, but not evidence of real-world accuracy. For that, see the real-data validation scored against published BLS observations.

signalToNoise.note: Signal is the price gap between the most and least FX-exposed category over the observed FX move. Noise is the AR(1) volatility remaining on a category mean after averaging over parts and months. Below an SNR of about 3 the ranking is not recoverable by any model, so a poor correlation is a property of the data rather than a failure of the estimator.

collinearity.note: Detectability and attributability are different questions. Over a near-monotonic depreciation the cumulative FX path is collinear with elapsed time, so a model cannot tell an FX effect from a trend effect no matter how large either is. Monthly returns carry the independent variation, which is why only returns are exposed as features. Separating FX properly needs a window containing reversals, or currencies that diverge.

mediation.interpretation: If the partial correlation shrinks toward zero relative to the total correlation, GPR's link to prices is largely mediated by freight / commodities / FX — consistent with the channel model.

dataSources.caveat: No public source publishes monthly piece prices per SKU per vendor per programme - that data lives only in OEM purchasing systems. This layer is simulated to specification and would be replaced by the customer's own purchase-order history.

drivers.name: FX spot rates (EUR/INR, USD/INR)
drivers.description: Exchange rate between the pricing currency and the currencies that imported content and global commodities are invoiced in.
drivers.impact_channel: Two channels. Direct: foreign-invoiced parts and sub-assemblies reprice one-for-one with the rate. Indirect: USD-benchmarked commodities raise input cost even for domestically bought parts.
drivers.direction: Domestic currency weakens -> imported input cost rises -> price rises, lagged 2-6 months
drivers.example: EUR/INR moved from 90.8 to 109.3 over the modelled window (+20.4%), which on a 95%-localised programme still lifts sensor and lighting categories materially because those are the content that stays imported.

sources.provider: Reserve Bank of India reference rate

drivers.name: FX forward curve / implied volatility
drivers.description: Market-implied expectations of future exchange rates, and the uncertainty around them.
drivers.impact_channel: Forward points are the market's own forecast of the driver we most care about. Implied volatility indicates how wide the forecast interval should be, which spot alone cannot tell you.
drivers.direction: Widening forward premium -> higher expected future input cost
drivers.example: A steep INR forward premium ahead of a known policy event signals expected depreciation before it shows up in spot.

drivers.name: Policy and lending rates
drivers.description: Central bank policy rate and corporate borrowing cost.
drivers.impact_channel: Working-capital cost for suppliers. Tier-2 and tier-3 vendors carrying inventory on credit pass financing cost into piece price, especially on long payment terms.
drivers.direction: Rates rise -> supplier financing cost rises -> upward price pressure
drivers.example: RBI repo rate changes feed vendor working-capital cost within roughly a quarter.

drivers.name: Internal FX hedging position
drivers.description: The company's own forward cover on foreign-currency payables.
drivers.impact_channel: Determines how much of an FX move actually reaches the P&L. A fully hedged quarter is insulated regardless of what spot does.
drivers.direction: Higher hedge ratio -> lower realised FX impact
drivers.example: A 70% hedged position converts a 10% depreciation into roughly a 3% realised cost increase.

drivers.name: Steel prices (HRC, CRC, alloy)
drivers.description: Hot and cold rolled coil, and alloy grades used in stampings, chassis and fasteners.
drivers.impact_channel: Dominant input cost for stampings, chassis, fasteners and brake components - often 50-70% of piece cost. Priced off global benchmarks even when bought domestically.
drivers.direction: Steel rises -> direct cost-up in steel-intensive categories, lagged by contract cadence
drivers.example: The 2021 HRC spike roughly doubled coil prices and triggered widespread cost-up claims across stamping vendors.

drivers.name: Aluminium and copper (LME)
drivers.description: Non-ferrous metals used in powertrain castings, HVAC, wiring harness and motors.
drivers.impact_channel: Copper drives wiring harness, alternators and motors; aluminium drives castings, heat exchangers and increasingly body structures. Both are exchange-traded, so pass-through is fast and visible.
drivers.direction: LME rises -> electrical and HVAC categories reprice within 1-3 months
drivers.example: Copper above $10,000/t materially raises harness and motor cost per vehicle.

drivers.name: Crude oil and polymer feedstock
drivers.description: Brent/WTI and downstream resins - PP, ABS, PA, PVC - used in trim and under-bonnet parts.
drivers.impact_channel: Polymer prices track crude with a one to two month lag. Interior trim, bumpers, hoses and sealing systems are polymer-dominated.
drivers.direction: Crude rises -> polymer feedstock rises -> trim and sealing categories rise, ~2 month lag
drivers.example: Interior trim and sealing categories track naphtha-linked resin contracts closely.

drivers.name: Rare earths and battery metals
drivers.description: Neodymium, dysprosium, lithium, cobalt, nickel - EV motors, batteries and sensors.
drivers.impact_channel: Permanent-magnet motors and battery packs. Supply is geographically concentrated, so price is as much a geopolitical variable as an industrial one.
drivers.direction: Supply restriction -> sharp, step-like increases in EV powertrain cost
drivers.example: China's 2023 export controls on gallium and germanium moved semiconductor and sensor input costs within weeks.

drivers.name: Industrial electricity and gas tariffs
drivers.description: Energy input cost for foundries, forging, heat treatment and paint shops.
drivers.impact_channel: Energy-intensive processes - casting, forging, glass, heat treatment - carry double-digit energy shares of conversion cost.
drivers.direction: Industrial tariff rises -> conversion cost rises in energy-intensive categories
drivers.example: The 2022 European gas crisis pushed energy surcharges into foundry and glass contracts across the continent.

drivers.name: Geopolitical risk / armed conflict
drivers.description: Quantified conflict and geopolitical tension, both globally and along specific sourcing corridors.
drivers.impact_channel: Conflict is an upstream driver rather than a direct one. It moves currency, energy, freight and insurance simultaneously - which is precisely why it is worth modelling separately: those channels are correlated during a shock in a way normal-times data will not show.
drivers.direction: Escalation -> currency weakness + energy spike + freight/insurance premium, compounding
drivers.example: Russia's invasion of Ukraine simultaneously moved palladium (catalytic converters), neon (semiconductor lithography), energy and wire harness supply out of western Ukraine - four separate channels from one event.

drivers.name: Import duties, tariffs and trade remedies
drivers.description: Customs duty rates, anti-dumping measures and countervailing duties on components and raw material.
drivers.impact_channel: A step change straight onto landed cost of imported content. Unlike most drivers this is discrete and dated - it is knowable in advance from the notification, which makes it unusually forecastable.
drivers.direction: Duty increase -> immediate step-up in landed cost of affected tariff lines
drivers.example: Indian customs duty changes on CKD kits and specific component lines land in the annual Union Budget with a known effective date.

drivers.name: Sanctions and export controls
drivers.description: Restrictions on specific materials, technologies, entities or destinations.
drivers.impact_channel: Forces resourcing to alternative suppliers, usually at higher cost and with requalification expense. Effect is a permanent level shift rather than a cyclical move.
drivers.direction: New control -> resourcing cost + qualification cost -> permanent step up
drivers.example: Semiconductor export controls reshaped ECU and sensor sourcing across the industry.

drivers.name: Free trade agreements and rules of origin
drivers.description: Preferential tariff access and the local-content thresholds required to claim it.
drivers.impact_channel: Determines the duty actually paid on imported content, and sets the localisation percentage that makes a programme FX-resilient in the first place.
drivers.direction: FTA in force -> lower effective duty on qualifying content
drivers.example: India-EFTA and India-UK agreements change the effective duty on European-sourced content.

drivers.name: Shipping chokepoint disruption
drivers.description: Suez/Red Sea, Panama Canal, Strait of Hormuz, Taiwan Strait transit status.
drivers.impact_channel: Rerouting adds transit days and freight cost, and forces air freight for line-stopping parts. Hits landed cost and lead time together.
drivers.direction: Chokepoint disruption -> freight + insurance + expedite cost, within weeks
drivers.example: Red Sea diversions from late 2023 added roughly 10-14 days to Asia-Europe transit and multiplied container rates.

drivers.name: Container freight rates
drivers.description: Spot and contract ocean freight on the lanes that carry imported content.
drivers.impact_channel: Direct landed-cost component for imported parts. Matters most for low-value/high-volume items where freight is a large share of delivered cost.
drivers.direction: Freight rates rise -> landed cost of imported content rises, 1-2 month lag
drivers.example: Drewry's composite index moved roughly 5x during 2021 and again during the 2024 Red Sea disruption.

drivers.name: Port congestion and dwell time
drivers.description: Berth waiting times and container dwell at origin and destination ports.
drivers.impact_channel: Lengthens lead time, forces safety stock, and triggers expedite premiums. Shows up as cost before it shows up as a freight rate.
drivers.direction: Congestion rises -> inventory carrying and expedite cost rise
drivers.example: JNPT and Nhava Sheva dwell times directly affect inbound schedules for Pune assembly.

drivers.name: Air freight rates
drivers.description: Air cargo cost, used for line-stopping and launch-critical parts.
drivers.impact_channel: The escape valve when ocean fails. Air freight cost is the true price of a supply disruption and is often absorbed invisibly in logistics budgets rather than piece price.
drivers.direction: Disruption -> air freight substitution -> sharp, temporary landed-cost spike
drivers.example: Semiconductor shortages routinely justified air freighting ECUs at many multiples of ocean cost.

drivers.name: Semiconductor lead times and allocation
drivers.description: MCU and power-semiconductor lead times, foundry utilisation and allocation status.
drivers.impact_channel: Allocation premiums and broker-market purchases. During shortage the spot price for a controller can exceed contract price many times over.
drivers.direction: Lead times extend -> allocation premium on electronics and sensors
drivers.example: The 2021-22 shortage produced broker prices at 10-100x contract for some automotive MCUs and idled assembly lines industry-wide.

drivers.name: Automotive parts price index
drivers.description: Published price index for motor vehicle parts - the sector's own inflation measure.
drivers.impact_channel: Captures the shared cost trend across the whole category that no single commodity explains: labour, overhead, margin and mix.
drivers.direction: Index rises -> broad upward pressure across all parts
drivers.example: The BLS motor vehicle parts index rose about 4.9% across the modelled window.

drivers.name: Domestic inflation (WPI / CPI)
drivers.description: Wholesale and consumer price inflation in the manufacturing country.
drivers.impact_channel: Most long-term supply agreements contain escalation clauses indexed to WPI. This is contractual pass-through, not an estimated effect.
drivers.direction: WPI rises -> contractual escalation triggers at the next reset
drivers.example: Indian LTAs commonly index conversion cost to WPI-manufactured with an annual reset.

drivers.name: Wage and labour cost index
drivers.description: Manufacturing wage growth and minimum wage revisions.
drivers.impact_channel: Conversion cost for labour-intensive operations - assembly, wiring harness, trim - where labour can exceed material cost.
drivers.direction: Wages rise -> conversion cost rises in labour-intensive categories
drivers.example: Harness assembly is labour-dominated, so state minimum wage revisions move it directly.

drivers.name: Industrial production index
drivers.description: Manufacturing output, as a proxy for capacity tightness across the supply base.
drivers.impact_channel: High utilisation across the supplier base reduces your negotiating leverage: a vendor running full has no reason to discount.
drivers.direction: High utilisation -> weaker buyer leverage -> firmer prices
drivers.example: IIP manufacturing above trend correlates with reduced willingness to accept cost-down.

drivers.name: Programme volume and take rate
drivers.description: Annual build volume per vehicle programme and per variant.
drivers.impact_channel: Piece price is contractually tiered on volume. This is usually the single largest controllable lever on unit cost.
drivers.direction: Volume rises -> next price tier -> lower piece price
drivers.example: A programme moving from 30k to 60k units per year typically unlocks a contractual tier.

drivers.name: Model lifecycle stage
drivers.description: Where a programme sits between launch, mid-cycle refresh and run-out.
drivers.impact_channel: Cost curves are lifecycle-dependent: launch carries tooling amortisation and low-volume premiums, maturity delivers learning-curve cost-down, run-out brings small-lot penalties back.
drivers.direction: Launch high -> maturity low -> run-out rises again
drivers.example: Tooling amortisation completing typically produces a visible one-off step down.

drivers.name: Seasonal demand pattern
drivers.description: Within-year demand cycles at category level.
drivers.impact_channel: Aftermarket and service demand peaks tighten supply for shared components, firming prices seasonally.
drivers.direction: Seasonal peak -> tighter supply -> firmer prices
drivers.example: Battery and lighting demand peaks in winter; cooling components peak pre-summer.

sources.provider: Derived from the price history itself

drivers.name: Powertrain mix shift (ICE to EV)
drivers.description: Share of build moving to electrified powertrains.
drivers.impact_channel: Structurally reshapes the parts basket: exhaust, fuel systems and transmissions decline while power electronics, magnets and thermal management grow. Declining-volume ICE parts get more expensive per unit as they lose scale.
drivers.direction: EV share rises -> ICE part volumes fall -> ICE piece cost rises on lost scale
drivers.example: Falling ICE volumes raise per-unit cost on exhaust and fuel system components.

drivers.name: Vendor profile and import dependency
drivers.description: Supplier origin, share of input cost that is foreign-invoiced, contract repricing cadence and price positioning.
drivers.impact_channel: Determines how much of any FX or commodity move a given vendor passes through, and how quickly. This is what makes exposure identifiable across suppliers within the same month.
drivers.direction: Higher import dependency -> larger and faster pass-through
drivers.example: International tier-1s in the modelled data carry roughly ten times the direct FX exposure of domestic vendors.

drivers.name: Supplier financial health
drivers.description: Credit rating, leverage, working-capital position and distress signals.
drivers.impact_channel: A distressed supplier either raises prices or fails. Both are cost events; the second is far more expensive because it forces emergency resourcing.
drivers.direction: Deteriorating health -> cost-up claims, or resourcing cost on failure
drivers.example: Tier-2 insolvencies during 2020-21 forced emergency resourcing at significant premiums.

drivers.name: Single-source and concentration risk
drivers.description: Number of qualified sources per part and geographic concentration of supply.
drivers.impact_channel: Single-sourced parts have no competitive tension, so cost-down is structurally harder and disruption risk is priced in.
drivers.direction: Single source -> weaker negotiating position -> firmer prices
drivers.example: Dual-sourcing a category typically unlocks competitive cost-down at the next negotiation.

drivers.name: Supplier capacity utilisation
drivers.description: How full a vendor's plant is relative to nameplate capacity.
drivers.impact_channel: A vendor running near capacity has no incentive to discount and may charge premiums for incremental volume.
drivers.direction: High utilisation -> firmer prices, longer lead times
drivers.example: Capacity-constrained casting suppliers routinely decline incremental volume at standard price.

drivers.name: Emission and safety regulation
drivers.description: Emission standards and mandated safety content.
drivers.impact_channel: Adds required content and forces redesign. Effect is a dated step change tied to the compliance deadline, not a gradual drift.
drivers.direction: New norm -> added content and redesign cost -> step up at the deadline
drivers.example: BS-VI raised aftertreatment content substantially; mandated six-airbag rules added restraint system cost across segments.

drivers.name: Localisation mandates and incentives
drivers.description: Production-linked incentive schemes and minimum local-content requirements.
drivers.impact_channel: Shifts the economics of importing versus localising, which in turn changes a programme's FX exposure profile.
drivers.direction: Incentive available -> localisation accelerates -> FX exposure falls
drivers.example: India's PLI scheme for auto components changed the make-versus-import calculus for several categories.

drivers.name: Carbon pricing and border adjustment
drivers.description: Emissions trading prices and carbon border adjustment mechanisms.
drivers.impact_channel: Adds cost to carbon-intensive inputs - steel, aluminium, glass - and to exports into jurisdictions operating a border adjustment.
drivers.direction: Carbon price rises -> steel and aluminium input cost rises
drivers.example: EU CBAM adds reporting and eventually cost to imported steel and aluminium content.

drivers.name: Part characteristics
drivers.description: Weight, dominant material, complexity tier and category classification.
drivers.impact_channel: Sets the baseline cost structure and determines which commodity a part is exposed to. A steel bracket and a semiconductor sensor of identical value respond to entirely different drivers.
drivers.direction: Determines which input cost drivers apply and in what proportion
drivers.example: Material composition decides whether a part tracks steel, copper or polymer.

drivers.name: Engineering change notices
drivers.description: Design changes affecting material, process or tolerance.
drivers.impact_channel: A direct, discrete repricing event. ECNs are the single most common cause of a price change that no market driver can explain.
drivers.direction: ECN issued -> renegotiated piece price at implementation
drivers.example: A tolerance tightening that forces an added machining operation raises piece cost immediately.

drivers.name: Tooling amortisation schedule
drivers.description: Remaining tooling cost recovered through piece price.
drivers.impact_channel: Amortisation completing produces a known, dated step down in piece price - fully predictable if the schedule is available.
drivers.direction: Amortisation completes -> step down in piece price
drivers.example: A part fully amortised at 200k units drops in price at that cumulative volume.

drivers.name: Contract structure and repricing cadence
drivers.description: Agreement type, repricing frequency, escalation clauses and cost-down commitments.
drivers.impact_channel: Determines when any input cost move is allowed to reach price. A vendor on an annual reset absorbs six months of commodity movement that a quarterly vendor passes on immediately.
drivers.direction: Longer reset -> slower, lumpier pass-through
drivers.example: Quarterly-reset vendors show FX pass-through roughly two quarters ahead of annual-reset vendors.

drivers.name: Payment terms and working capital
drivers.description: Days payable and any early-payment discount structure.
drivers.impact_channel: Extended terms shift financing cost onto the supplier, who prices it back in. The saving is usually smaller than the price increase.
drivers.direction: Longer payment terms -> supplier financing cost -> higher piece price
drivers.example: Moving from 60 to 120 day terms typically returns as a piece-price increase.

drivers.name: Negotiation and cost-down calendar
drivers.description: Scheduled annual negotiations and committed year-on-year cost-down targets.
drivers.impact_channel: Produces predictable, dated step changes. Much of the observable price movement in a mature programme is calendar-driven rather than market-driven.
drivers.direction: Negotiation round -> committed cost-down applied on the effective date
drivers.example: A committed 3% annual cost-down applied each April is fully predictable from the calendar.
